---
title: "Extending qmd-fast"
---

This chapter is for working *on* qmd-fast: the conventions, where new code goes,
the extension points, and the dev loop.

## The guiding principle: a lean core

The core stays small and predictable; power lives at the edges. Before adding to
the core, ask whether it can be an **extension** or a **client enhancer** instead.
Server-side transforms (parsing, the block model, the diff) belong in the core;
presentation and optional features should ride the extension points below.

## Conventions

- **Rust edition 2024**, workspace resolver 3. Shared dependencies are declared
  once in the root `[workspace.dependencies]` so versions stay centralized.
- **Directory-module pattern.** When a file grows past ~1.5k lines it becomes a
  directory module: a `mod.rs` plus focused submodules that reach shared items via
  `use super::*` and expose what the parent needs as `pub(super)`. `render/` and
  `site/` are split this way.
- **The block contract is load-bearing.** Anything you emit must keep
  `data-block-id` (content hash) + `data-sourcepos` (and `data-source-file` for
  includes). Source mapping, the diff, and live-state preservation all key off it.
- **`rustfmt`-clean, `clippy`-clean.** A `PostToolUse` hook formats every edited
  `.rs`; CI enforces `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo test`, `cargo clippy -D warnings`,
  and a weekly `cargo audit`.

## Where a change goes

| You want to… | Touch |
|---|---|
| Change how a markdown element renders | `render/emit.rs` (+ `divs.rs`/`figure.rs` for those) |
| Add a pipeline stage | `render/mod.rs` (`render_internal`), keeping it source-map-preserving |
| Change incremental behaviour | `diff.rs` |
| Add a site/book feature | `site/` |
| Change code execution / the kernel | `server/exec.rs`, `server/kernel.rs` |
| Add a client-side behaviour | a JS enhancer (below), not the core |

## The three extension points

These let features live *outside* the core (see [Extensions](../guide/using/extensions.html)
in the User Guide for the authoring side):

1. **Format extensions** (`render/extension/`). `_extensions/<name>/_extension.yml`
   contributes includes, a theme, and resources to a base format. A failed load is
   reported through the `warnings` channel, never silent.
2. **Declarative shortcodes** (`render/extension/`). A flat, top-level `shortcodes:`
   map in `_extension.yml` maps a name to an HTML template, expanded at pipeline
   stage 2. The manifest is a **closed set**: any key outside `NATIVE_MANIFEST_KEYS`
   is flagged with a did-you-mean hint, so the old Quarto `contributes.shortcodes`
   nesting is no longer read (it warns as an unknown manifest key). Two shortcodes are
   **built in** and need no extension: `{{< embed deck.qmd >}}` (embed another document's
   deck as an isolating iframe) and `{{< video clip.mp4 [dark=…] >}}` (a theme-matched
   `<video>` authored in Markdown). An extension template of the same name takes
   precedence, since the built-ins are `render_shortcode` fallbacks.
3. **Client enhancers** (`window.qmdEnhancers`, in `code-enhance.js`). An
   extension's JS registers `fn(root)` that runs after every (re)mount. The
   built-in copy buttons and `mermaid.js` use this same public API, so a
   third-party enhancer is indistinguishable from core's.

### The client enhancer contract

An **enhancer** is a `function(root)` that decorates freshly-mounted DOM. It is the only
sanctioned way to add client-side behaviour, and the contract is small enough to state in
full:

- **Register** with `window.qmdEnhancers.register(fn)`. `fn` receives a `root` element
  (the just-mounted subtree, or `document` for a whole-page run); scope your queries to
  it (`root.querySelectorAll(...)`), not to `document`, so an incremental update only
  re-decorates the block that changed.
- **When it runs.** The same `fn` fires on three occasions: once on the **initial full
  render** (`DOMContentLoaded` in a static build, the `full_render` snapshot in the live
  preview), again **after every incremental block op** (the client calls
  `qmdEnhancers.run(root)` on the swapped-in DOM, so a re-rendered block is enhanced just
  like a fresh one), and **immediately on registration** if the page is already mounted
  (the case when an extension script loads late in `include-after-body`).
- **Idempotency is mandatory.** Because the same `fn` re-runs on every change, it must do
  nothing the second time it sees a node. The convention is a marker `data-` attribute:
  check for it, bail if present, set it once you've decorated. An enhancer that appends a
  button without this guard will stack a new button on every keystroke.
- **Failures are contained.** Each enhancer runs inside a `try/catch`; a throw is logged
  to the console (`[qmd] enhancer failed`) and the other enhancers still run. An enhancer
  bug degrades one decoration, it does not blank the page.

A minimal, idempotent enhancer that adds a "Run" affordance to every `pre.shell` block:

```js
window.qmdEnhancers.register(function (root) {
  root.querySelectorAll('pre.shell:not([data-ran])').forEach(function (pre) {
    pre.dataset.ran = '1';                 // guard: only decorate once
    var btn = document.createElement('button');
    btn.textContent = 'Run';
    btn.addEventListener('click', function () { /* ... */ });
    pre.appendChild(btn);
  });
});
```

Ship that file as a `resources:` entry of an extension and inject it (typically via the
extension's `body-end:`), and it is wired into the same mount cycle the built-ins use.

### How a format extension loads

`format: <name>-revealjs` (or `-html`) names a base format plus an installed
extension. The renderer (`render/extension/`) reads
`_extensions/<name>/_extension.yml`, applies the extension's `theme:` *on top of*
the base theme (so the extension restyles rather than replaces), and injects the
includes and resources its manifest declares, resolving resource paths inside the
extension's own sub-directory. The core stays a **thin injector**: the extension
supplies the CSS/JS, the core just wires it in (and reports a failed load through
`warnings`, never silently). This is what lets a theme extension restyle qmd-fast's
own [deck engine](deck-engine.qmd) against its native `.qmd-deck` contract.

Besides that `format: <name>-base` form, an extension can be activated
**format-agnostically** with an `extensions: [a, b]` front-matter list, merged in order
so a later one wins. That is how a plain `format: html` page pulls in a shortcode pack or
a theme without naming a base format.

#### Where the extension is found

Both forms resolve the directory the same way (`find_extension_dir` in
`render/extension/`): starting from the page's own directory, qmd-fast looks for
`_extensions/<name>/_extension.yml` and, if it isn't there, **walks up toward the
filesystem root**, trying `_extensions/<name>/` at each parent. The first hit wins. So a
chapter buried at `book/part-two/ch-7.qmd` finds an extension vendored once at the project
root (`book/_extensions/<name>/`), not only one copied next to the page.

That walk-up is also why nested books behave: each book is its own project rooted at its
`_site.yml`, and the search bottoms out at whichever `_extensions/` it reaches first
climbing from the page, so a sibling book's extensions never leak in by accident. When no
`_extensions/<name>/` is found anywhere up the tree, the lookup falls back to the
**page-relative** path so the not-found warning still names a sensible location.

#### When a load fails

A `format:`/`extensions:` reference that names an extension whose manifest can't be read
or parsed is an **authoring mistake worth surfacing**, not a silent no-op:
`load_manifest` pushes a located entry onto the `warnings` channel (`format extension
'<name>' not found (looked for …)` or `could not parse …`) and the page **still renders**
without the contribution. Likewise, the manifest is a closed set: any top-level key
outside `NATIVE_MANIFEST_KEYS` warns with a did-you-mean hint. Nothing in an extension's
load path aborts the render; the worst case is a page that renders unstyled plus a warning
in the dev menu / build log.

## Editor integration: the VS Code companion

The websocket protocol is open (see [the block model](block-model.qmd)), so an editor
that hosts the preview is just another thin client, not a fork. One such client already
ships in-repo, at `editor/vscode/`: the **qmd-fast Companion**. It is the concrete
*producer* for the reverse-sync side of the protocol that `web-client/client.js` already
*consumes*, so the two halves meet.

It lives **outside the cargo workspace** with its own npm/esbuild toolchain (`cd
editor/vscode && npm install && npm run build`, then **F5** to launch an Extension
Development Host). A single command, `qmdFast.openPreview` (command palette or the
editor-title button on a `.qmd`), and one setting, `qmdFast.path` (the binary, when
`qmd-fast` is not on `PATH`), are its whole surface.

The host architecture is deliberately thin:

- it spawns `qmd-fast preview` on a free **localhost** port (no `--host`, so the LAN
  token never enters the picture) and embeds that URL in a webview via
  `vscode.env.asExternalUri`;
- a small **relay** HTML document inside the webview bridges the preview iframe's
  `postMessage` protocol to and from the extension host. Forward sync (`qmd-goto`) calls
  `revealRange` to move the editor cursor; reverse sync turns a cursor move into a
  debounced `qmd-cursor`, which the client resolves with `highlightAtLine` (and, in a
  deck, jumps `QmdDeck` to the containing slide).

The companion **never writes back to the source**: it only navigates and highlights,
holding the line that the `.qmd` file is the single editing surface and the preview is a
read-only view. Phase 1 is exactly this host-plus-cursor loop, localhost only; editor
*commands* that transform the buffer (insert-block, reorder-slide) are deferred to a
later phase, and strictly as `.qmd`-text transforms when they land.

## Recipes

### Add a new cell option

Cell options (`#| key: value`, `//|` for `{js}`, `%%|` for `{mermaid}`) are a **closed
vocabulary**: any key not in the recognized set warns with a did-you-mean hint at its
exact source line. So adding one is two steps, in order.

1. **Stop the warning.** Add the key to `CELL_OPTION_KEYS` in `render/validate.rs` (a flat
   `&[&str]`). This is the single list `validate_cell_options` checks; until the key is
   there, every author who uses it gets `unknown cell option \`yourkey\``. The list is the
   union across all cell languages, so a `{js}`-only option lives here too (`name`,
   `viewof`, `input` already do).

2. **Read it where cells are processed.** The key is now *allowed* but still *inert*. Two
   places consume options depending on what the option does:
   - **Render-time** options (presentation: `code-fold`, `code-summary`,
     `code-line-numbers`, `label`, `fig-cap`) are read in the render pipeline as the cell's
     HTML is emitted (`render/mod.rs` parses the leading `#|` block; `emit.rs` applies the
     code-fold / line-number wrappers). Add your read there if the option only changes how
     the cell or its output looks.
   - **Execution-time** options (`echo`, `include`, `cache`, `fig-export`) are read in
     `server/exec.rs`, where each is captured onto the per-cell `CellRef` before the run
     and consulted while planning what re-runs. Add your read there if the option changes
     *whether or how* a cell runs.

A render-only option needs no kernel and shows up immediately in `render`/`check`; an
execution option only takes effect under `preview`/`build` with a live kernel. Pin the new
option with a corpus document that uses it (the corpus is the spec), and `check` will keep
it from regressing into an unknown-key warning.

::: {.callout-note}
The parser only reads the **leading contiguous** `#|` block: the first non-option line
stops option parsing. A `#|` comment further down the cell body is just code, not an
option, so your new key has to appear at the top of the cell.
:::

### Write a figure file on execution: `#| fig-export:`

`#| fig-export: figures/x.pdf` (a comma-separated list for several files at once, e.g. a
vector `.pdf` plus a raster `.png`) is the path through `exec.rs` worth understanding
because it touches three things at once: the executor, the cache key, and the kernel
preamble.

- **It is executor-side, not a render transform.** For a Python cell, `export_wrapped`
  (`server/exec.rs`) prepends a one-line `_qmd_export([...], install=True)` trigger to the
  cell's code before sending it to the kernel. The `_qmd_export` hook itself is defined
  once in the Python preamble (`server/kernel.rs`); `install=True` makes it idempotently
  wrap the figure even for a cell that produces a plot without naming matplotlib directly.
- **Paths are relative to the document directory.** The warm kernel's working directory is
  the document's own directory (`kernel.rs`), so an exported `figures/x.pdf`, like any
  other file a cell writes (`ggsave`, an audio file), lands beside the source where the
  build can find and copy it.
- **It is written at display time, before any inline recolour.** The figure is saved
  print-clean (real black axes/text for LaTeX/print) the moment the plot is displayed,
  *before* the light/dark inline recolouring that produces the `.qmd-fig-light` /
  `.qmd-fig-dark` pair the page swaps on a theme change. So the on-disk file is a clean
  print artifact, not a theme-tinted screen image.
- **It is folded into the cache key.** The export spec is appended to the cell's hashed
  code (`# qmd-fig-export: <spec>`), so adding or changing it **moves the cell's
  cumulative hash** and forces a re-run, which rewrites the file. A cell *without*
  `fig-export:` hashes exactly as before, so existing `_freeze/` entries stay valid. This
  is what guarantees the exported file is never stale relative to the cell that produced
  it.

## The dev loop

```sh
cargo run -p taliesin-server -- preview corpus/<doc>   # iterate on a real doc
cargo test -p taliesin-core                            # corpus invariants + unit tests
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cd web-client && npx -y -p typescript tsc -p jsconfig.json   # type-check client.js
```

### The corpus is the spec

There is no exhaustive feature checklist. The contract is that the real documents
under `corpus/` render correctly; `crates/core/tests/corpus.rs` asserts the block
invariants across all of them. Add a representative document to the corpus when you
add a feature.

### Byte-identity for refactors

A pure refactor must not change the output. The standard check is to build the
corpus before and after and `diff` the results:

```sh
qmd-fast build corpus/tech-blog --out /tmp/before/site   # on the old tree
qmd-fast build corpus/tech-blog --out /tmp/after/site    # on the new tree
diff -rq /tmp/before /tmp/after                          # must be empty
```

That, plus the test suite, is what makes the larger module splits safe.
